-87.63900,41.89450.name: Institute for Human Reproduction (IHR)
-87.63900,41.89450.desc: A fertility clinic reporting to the CDC's National ART Surveillance System. Medical director: David P. Cohen, MD. A fertility clinic is where human embryos are made, selected and stored, and where assisted reproduction happens, like IVF, ICSI, egg and sperm donation, freezing embryos and eggs for later. Reporting is required of every US clinic performing assisted reproduction, under the Fertility Clinic Success Rate and Certification Act, so this is close to a complete register rather than a list of members. What it records is cycles started, which is not the same as children born.

-75.72059,45.39419.status: Certificate of GAP Last visit: interim, January 2026
-75.72059,45.39419.desc: An institution certified by the Canadian Council on Animal Care for its use of animals in science. Certificate of GAP Last visit: interim, January 2026. CCAC certification is a condition of federal research funding rather than a licence, so an institution outside it is not necessarily outside the work — it may simply not take federal money. The CCAC publishes names and certificate status and no addresses, so this point marks the institution rather than the building where animals are held.

-99.13320,19.43260.name: CIBIOGEM
-99.13320,19.43260.desc: Mexico’s biosafety commission, which sits over the most consequential dispute in this field: Mexico is where maize was domesticated, and engineered maize found in Oaxacan landraces is not contamination of a crop but of the reservoir every commercial maize variety on Earth was ultimately bred from. Mexico’s decree restricting GM maize for human consumption was challenged by the United States under the USMCA trade agreement, which is where a country’s biosafety decision gets tested against its trade obligations.

-99.13320,19.43260.name: CONAHCYT — native maize and public research
-99.13320,19.43260.desc: Mexico’s national science council, funding research on native maize varieties and supporting the government’s position on GM maize imports. Public research money directed at landraces rather than at commercial varieties is unusual and deliberate here.

-99.13320,19.43260.name: Demanda Colectiva en Defensa del Maíz Nativo
-99.13320,19.43260.state: Mexico City — Twelfth Federal District Court for Civil Matters
-99.13320,19.43260.desc: Fifty-three farmer, consumer and environmental organisations filed a collective action in July 2013 arguing that engineered maize threatened the native varieties of the crop's centre of origin, and that the constitution's guarantee of a healthy environment covered it. A precautionary measure issued that September halted every authorisation to plant engineered maize in Mexico. What makes this the most instructive case on the map is what happened next: the government and the companies brought roughly a hundred legal challenges, producing 22 amparo judgments resolved by 17 different federal courts and by the Supreme Court, and the measure survived all of them. In 2017 the Court's First Chamber declined even to docket Monsanto's appeal. A precautionary suspension that is cheap to obtain and expensive to overturn is a different instrument from a ban, and this is the worked example of it.

-99.13320,19.43260.name: Suprema Corte de Justicia de la Nación — surrogacy, 2021
-99.13320,19.43260.desc: In 2021 Mexico's supreme court held surrogacy to be a protected medical procedure under the constitutional right to form a family, and to be equally accessible regardless of gender, marital status or sexual orientation. The ruling upheld a surrogate's right to be compensated and displaced state-level restrictions, including one state's exclusion of foreigners. The effect was the opposite of every other movement recorded in this facet: while Thailand, Nepal, India, Cambodia and Russia were closing to foreign intended parents and Georgia was announcing the same, a constitutional court opened a jurisdiction. Only two states have since passed explicit regulations, so elsewhere in the country the arrangement runs through individual court orders — a right established nationally and administered case by case.

121.24000,14.16900.name: MASIPAG
121.24000,14.16900.desc: A Philippine network of farmers and scientists breeding rice varieties collectively and keeping them out of the patent system, and one of the petitioners in the case that revoked the Golden Rice approval. It is the clearest example of farmers doing the breeding themselves rather than choosing between varieties others have bred, which is a different argument from opposing a technology. The Court of Appeals revoked the Golden Rice commercial propagation permit in April 2024 and ordered UPLB to cease propagating Bt eggplant; the government petitioned the Supreme Court that October. A developer was enjoined directly rather than through the agency that licensed it.

-93.60000,41.90000.name: StarLink maize — unapproved variety in the human food supply
-93.60000,41.90000.desc: A maize approved only for animal feed turned up in taco shells and hundreds of other foods, triggering a nationwide recall in 2000. It had entered the human supply through ordinary grain handling, and the episode is why segregating an approved-for-feed-only crop is now generally treated as impossible in practice.

8.66000,49.88000.name: Merck KGaA / MilliporeSigma
8.66000,49.88000.desc: Holds CRISPR patents granted in Europe, Canada and elsewhere while the American dispute ran, and supplies a large share of the reagents laboratories buy daily. The same technique therefore has different owners in different jurisdictions, so where an experiment happens decides who is owed for it — a fact about patent law rather than about biology.

77.39000,13.10000.name: Bioneeds India
77.39000,13.10000.desc: A preclinical contract research organisation on a five-acre campus outside Bengaluru with around 250,000 square feet of built space, plus separate chemistry and biopharma laboratories. It states more than 23,500 good laboratory practice studies submitted to regulators worldwide over sixteen years, breeds its own rats, mice, guinea pigs and rabbits, and is certified under India's national GLP authority, approved by the national animal experiments committee, and accredited by the international laboratory animal care body. Its client range covers pharmaceuticals, vaccines, biologics, medical devices, agrochemicals and industrial chemicals — the same facility producing the safety data behind a crop protection product and a gene therapy. Regulators in a dozen countries read those studies; none of them inspects this campus, and the accreditations are what stands in place of that.

-122.27300,37.87150.name: The Sperm Bank of California
-122.27300,37.87150.desc: Founded in 1982, the only non-profit sperm bank in the United States, and the counter-example this facet needed. Where no law sets a ceiling on children per donor, it sets its own at ten families — the lowest nationally, against limits of twenty, forty and more elsewhere — and states plainly what undermines even that: unreported pregnancies, delayed reporting, and vials or embryos held at clinics without its knowledge. It created the Identity-Release programme in 1983, the first open-identity scheme anywhere, and in 2014 stopped offering permanently anonymous donation altogether after feedback from donor-conceived adults. It tracks pregnancies and birth outcomes, publishes research on the families it helps create, and employs an ethicist. Every constraint here is voluntary, which is exactly the point: the same absence of law that let one donor father hundreds of children lets another organisation cap itself at ten.
